books.section: Students for a Democratic Society and the Rise of the New Left
The New Left, Feminism, and the Counterculture

primary_sources: Mario Savio, ‘Bodies Upon the Gears’ speech, December 2, 1964 (paraphrased)
Twenty-sixth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, ratified July 1, 1971
National Center for Education Statistics, Table 303.10

source: original; documents are paraphrases of public sources (see each document’s sourcing note); the table is from the National Center for Education Statistics; the photographs are public domain

stimulus.source_note: DBQ: documents below are the stimulus.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which young people challenged the values of the postwar consensus in the 1960s.

documents.title: A manifesto for participation
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Port Huron Statement, adopted by Students for a Democratic Society, June 1962.
documents.sourcing: The statement is a student manifesto, so it states the movement’s aims in its own hopeful terms.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the Port Huron Statement, adopted by Students for a Democratic Society at its first national convention in Port Huron, Michigan, in June 1962. The statement says American society has failed to live up to its promises of peace and justice. It calls for a ‘democracy of individual participation,’ in which ordinary people share in the decisions that shape their lives, and it says students must lead the change.

documents.title: Stop the machine
documents.source: Paraphrase of Mario Savio’s speech at the University of California, Berkeley, December 2, 1964.
documents.sourcing: Savio spoke to a rally about to occupy a building, so his words are a call to action, not a calm analysis.
documents.text: Paraphrase of Mario Savio’s speech at Sproul Hall, University of California, Berkeley, December 2, 1964. Savio told the rally that the university was run like a machine. When its workings became unbearable, he said, students had to block them with their own bodies to bring the machine to a halt.

documents.title: Four mop-tops
documents.source: Photograph: The Beatles in 1964, by Bernard Gotfryd, public domain (Library of Congress).
documents.sourcing: The studio portraits show the band as its managers presented it: matching suits and matching hair.

documents.title: Turn on, tune in, drop out
documents.source: Account of Timothy Leary’s speech at the Human Be-In, Golden Gate Park, San Francisco, January 14, 1967.
documents.sourcing: Leary spoke to a friendly crowd of hippies, so his words preach to believers rather than persuade skeptics.
documents.text: At the Human Be-In in Golden Gate Park, Timothy Leary told a crowd of about 30,000 that they should ‘Turn on, tune in, drop out.’ Leary, a former Harvard professor who promoted the psychedelic drug LSD, urged young people to leave mainstream life behind and seek inner experience instead.

documents.title: On Haight Street
documents.source: Photograph: young people on Haight Street, San Francisco, printed in The Greenville News, April 30, 1967, public domain.
documents.sourcing: The newspaper photograph shows the hippies as outsiders saw them: a street scene, not a portrait the hippies posed for.

documents.title: Woodstock and Altamont
documents.source: Account of the Woodstock and Altamont festivals, 1969, drawn from the grounding books.
documents.sourcing: The account is written after both festivals, so it judges Woodstock by what Altamont showed next.
documents.text: In August 1969, more than 400,000 young people gathered at Woodstock for three days of rock music, far more than the 50,000 the promoters had expected. Four months later, a free festival at Altamont Speedway in California ended in disorganization and violence, and a concertgoer was stabbed and killed during the Rolling Stones’ set.

documents.title: More students than ever
documents.source: Table: Total fall enrollment in degree-granting colleges and universities, National Center for Education Statistics, Table 303.10.
documents.sourcing: The table counts enrollment; it does not say what the new students believed.
documents.text: 1961: 4,145,065. 1965: 5,920,864. 1970: 8,580,887. College enrollment more than doubled during the 1960s, as baby-boom students filled expanding universities.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which young people challenged the values of the postwar consensus in the 1960s, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as postwar prosperity and suburban conformity, the Cold War consensus, or the civil rights movement of the early 1960s.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (first point): earns the point for describing specific examples from at least three documents that support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without using their content, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (outside evidence): earns the point for describing at least one specific piece of evidence beyond the documents that supports the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Repeating a document’s content as outside evidence does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience of at least one document shapes what it says.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document’s author without explaining how that shapes the document does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for showing a complex understanding, such as explaining both the challenge and its limits, or qualifying the argument with evidence that cuts the other way.
rubric.notEarned: A one-sided argument with no qualification or counter-evidence does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Young people challenged the values of the postwar consensus deeply — in politics, culture, and daily life — but the challenge stayed partial. Background: Mainstream America pushed back, and the market absorbed much of the rebellion.
Grouping: Documents 1-2 show the political challenge (Port Huron, Savio); Documents 3-5 show the cultural challenge (Beatles, Leary, Haight Street); Documents 6-7 show the scale and the limits (Woodstock and Altamont, enrollment).
Outside evidence: Background: The Twenty-sixth Amendment, ratified July 1, 1971, lowered the voting age to 18 after young men argued they were old enough to fight and old enough to vote; the Free Speech Movement’s tactics spread to the Columbia University protests of 1968 and the student strike after Kent State in 1970.
Complexity: Background: The same decade that filled Haight-Ashbury also elected Richard Nixon in 1968 on an appeal to the ‘silent majority,’ and the music the counterculture made became big business. Background: Woodstock’s promoters had expected 50,000 and got more than 400,000, so youth culture was a market as well as a movement.
